analysis.one_liner: Raises corporate tax rates for companies whose CEO pay is more than 50 times their median worker's pay.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would add a 0.5 to 5 percentage-point surcharge on the 21% corporate tax rate for companies with CEO-to-worker pay ratios above 50 to 1, was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on September 11, 2025 and has had no hearing or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill raises the corporate tax rate on large companies where the CEO or highest-paid employee earns more than 50 times what the median worker makes. The surcharge starts at half a percentage point and rises with the pay gap, reaching 5 extra percentage points for companies above a 500-to-1 ratio. Companies that narrow the gap — by raising typical workers' pay or slowing executive pay growth — pay less.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at large corporations with wide pay gaps gain the most, because their employers now have a direct tax reason to raise median wages or slow CEO pay growth. Taxpayers gain from the revenue the surcharge raises on companies that keep extreme pay ratios. Workers broadly gain from the reporting: companies over $100 million in receipts that don't even file with the SEC would have to calculate and report their pay ratio for the first time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers at large corporations with wide pay gaps

how_it_helps.text: Adds a tiered surcharge to the 21% corporate rate: half a point for pay ratios above 50-to-1, rising one point per extra 100-to-1 of gap, up to 5 additional points for ratios above 500-to-1.
Uses a 5-year averaged version of the SEC's existing pay-ratio disclosure, so companies can't dodge the tax with one unusual year.

Extends the pay-ratio requirement to private companies with at least $100 million in average annual receipts, which are otherwise exempt from SEC disclosure rules, so large private firms can't escape by staying unlisted.
Directs the Treasury Department to write rules preventing companies from gaming the ratio, including by replacing employees with outside contractors.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations with high CEO-to-worker pay ratios pay a higher corporate tax rate — 21.5% to 26% depending on the gap. The cost lands mostly on shareholders of big publicly traded companies and on large private firms. Companies can avoid the surcharge entirely by narrowing their pay gap, so it functions as a standing tax on extreme pay ratios rather than a fixed cost.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations with wide CEO pay gaps

drawbacks.text: A company can simply keep its extreme pay ratio and pay the tax. At the lowest tier the increase is only half a percentage point on a 21% rate, and even the top tier is 5 points, so for the most profitable firms the surcharge may be cheaper than raising median wages across the workforce.

Large private companies that have never had to report a pay ratio would face new calculation and reporting costs; measuring median worker compensation across a big workforce is administratively complex.

The design depends on Treasury regulations to stop companies from manipulating the ratio — for example by shifting workers to contractor status — and the bill only directs Treasury to write those rules, so the anti-avoidance protection is only as good as the regulations that follow.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is simple and well-aimed: it uses a pay figure companies already report to the SEC, exempts small private firms, and tries to close the contractor loophole up front. Its honest weakness is that it pressures rather than forces — the penalty is modest, so a highly profitable company with a 400-to-1 ratio could treat it as a rounding error. As a result the bill is more likely to shift behavior at the margins and raise revenue from the worst offenders than to compress pay gaps across the economy.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day after it was introduced and has sat there with no hearing, markup, or vote since; Congress is still in session, so it could still move, but nothing has happened.

narrative.text: Representative Rashida Tlaib introduced the bill on September 11, 2025, with 20 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee, which writes tax law, on September 11, 2025.
Twenty-nine House Democrats had signed on as cosponsors, with no Republican support, and the committee has taken no action since the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with extreme CEO-to-worker pay ratios are better off so far, because the higher tax rate has not advanced toward a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High pay-ratio corporations that avoid the tax

for.name: 29 of 217 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors such as Jim McGovern, Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, and Ayanna Pressley

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Jason Smith)
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction for tax bills
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred on September 11, 2025 — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled

against.name: House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Has not brought the bill to the floor, and no Republican has cosponsored it

sides.party_line_note: All 30 sponsors and cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the Republican-led Ways and Means Committee has not acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Large publicly traded corporations with high pay ratios (big retail, tech, finance, healthcare)
industries.note: These firms face a 0.5 to 5 percentage-point higher corporate tax rate unless they shrink the gap between CEO and median-worker pay. Their financial interest in keeping the gap wide runs directly against the bill's goal of narrowing it.

industries.industry: Corporate executives and other highest-paid employees
industries.note: The bill counts the highest-paid employee, not just the CEO, so surcharge exposure pushes companies to slow growth in top compensation. Executive pay is the main lever companies could pull to avoid the tax.

They gain an exemption if they stay under the $100 million receipts threshold, but above it they must calculate and report a pay ratio for the first time and face the same surcharge — a new compliance cost and tax exposure.
New pay-ratio calculations for large private companies and annual surcharge computations create billable compliance work.

analysis.trajectory: The bill is very likely to die in the Ways and Means Committee without a vote. It has no Republican cosponsors, the committee and the floor are controlled by the Republican majority, and tax bills almost never reach the House floor without the committee chair scheduling action. The best realistic path is inclusion as a provision in a broader tax package, which the sponsor could pursue if the party ever controls the committee.
